holes_found.description: Year-count vs. attribution mismatch in detail_verdict_text. The rewrite says 'Edmund Halley\'s late-17th-century declination surveys — roughly 390 years of public record.' But Halley's Atlantic chart published 1701 and his voyages 1698-1700 are 325-328 years before 2026, not ~390. The 390-year figure actually anchors to Henry Gellibrand's 1634-35 discovery of magnetic secular variation (2026 - 1635 = 391 years). A dome defender could pick: 'Either the 390-year figure is wrong and you mean 325, or your attribution is wrong and you mean Gellibrand 1635, not Halley.' The argument is unharmed but the citation precision is loose.
holes_found.recommendation: Two options: (a) keep '390 years' and re-attribute to 'Henry Gellibrand\'s 1634 secular-variation discovery' (with Halley's later surveys as the canonical systematic record); or (b) keep Halley attribution and tighten to '~325 years of systematic public record (since Halley\'s 1698-1701 declination voyages)'. Option (a) is the historically defensible 'public record' anchor for the post-hoc-test argument; option (b) is the safer rhetorical citation. Prefer (a).

holes_found.description: Internal inconsistency between detail_evidence and detail_verdict_text Halley date-range. detail_evidence says 'since Edmund Halley\'s late-17th/early-18th-century declination surveys' (correct — voyages 1698-1700, chart 1701). detail_verdict_text says 'Edmund Halley\'s late-17th-century declination surveys' (truncates the early-18th-century part, which is actually where Halley's main published declination work sits). The fields disagree on the same author, same surveys.
holes_found.recommendation: Make the verdict text match the evidence text: 'late-17th/early-18th-century declination surveys'. One-line patch.

stronger_arguments.description: If the rewrite adopts option (a) above (attribute to Gellibrand 1634-35), the post-hoc argument actually becomes stronger because Gellibrand's discovery is specifically the discovery of secular variation — i.e., the discovery that magnetic declination CHANGES OVER TIME. That's structurally identical to the 'westward drift' phenomenon. The dome's claim 'we predict SAA western drift' is then transparently identical to claiming you 'predict' Gellibrand's 391-year-old discovery — which makes the post-hoc-test point ('not plausibly known to the author at write-time') vivid rather than just numerically true.
sources: Gellibrand, H. (1635), 'A Discourse Mathematical on the Variation of the Magneticall Needle', London — first published demonstration of secular variation
Halley, E. (1701), 'A New and Correct Chart Shewing the Variations of the Compass in the Western and Southern Oceans' — first systematic geomagnetic chart

kernel_of_truth.description: Westward SAA-western-cell drift is a real, multi-century-tracked phenomenon (data/wins.json WIN-060 detail_evidence: 'documented since Edmund Halley\'s late-17th/early-18th-century declination surveys'). The dome is engaging with real geomagnetic data — INTERMAGNET, Swarm L1B, NOAA WMM2025, ESA IGRF-14 — and the direction (westward) is uncontroversial.
kernel_of_truth.why_it_doesnt_save_claim: But the verdict 'Std Model Explains' rests on the dome having no INDEPENDENT mechanism to predict the rate (data/wins.json WIN-060 finding: 'It has no core-flow mechanism to predict drift rate or direction independently'). Standard MHD via Finlay 2016 derives the rate from CMB flow inversions; the dome only extrapolates the same NOAA/ESA data. And the post-hoc paragraph (data/wins.json WIN-060 detail_verdict_text) sharpens this by anchoring to a centuries-old public record: a 2026 'prediction' of a 390-year-old observable cannot be prospective, regardless of any timestamping mechanism. The rewrite separates the disqualifier (age of observable) from the symptom (no monitor.py entry), which preempts the defender pivot 'we just haven\'t added it to monitor.py yet'.

- NEW post-hoc carve-out: 'requires that the data be "not plausibly known to the author at write-time," which a 390-year-old indexed observable plainly cannot satisfy — adopting it as a 2026 prediction is the disqualifier, not the absence of a timestamp.'

advocate_mode.best_defense: A fair-minded dome defender's strongest line: 'Your post-hoc argument hinges on "public record" age, but the modern QUANTITATIVE drift rate (0.18-0.24°/yr depending on epoch) was only nailed down via satellite-era inversions — POMME, CHAOS, Finlay 2016, Swarm L1B 2013-2024. The dome\'s prediction is consistency with those modern values, not with Gellibrand\'s qualitative observation that declination changes. Comparing to a 390-year-old qualitative phenomenon is a category error — "westward drift exists" is 390 years old; "westward drift is X°/yr to ±0.02" is decades old at most.'
advocate_mode.preemptive_recommendation: The rewrite already partially handles this: 'the modern rate is tabulated to high precision in NOAA\'s WMM2025 and ESA\'s IGRF-14' acknowledges the modern-quantitative axis. But it could explicitly say: 'Even granting the dome is predicting a modern quantitative rate rather than the qualitative observable, that rate has been continuously tabulated since IGRF-1 in 1968 and updated via 5-year IGRF generations — also publicly indexed years before the V51 monitor commit.' That preempts the category-error pivot without bloating the paragraph.
